source.title: Best practice for motor imagery: a systematic literature review on motor imagery training elements in five different disciplines

paper.citation: Schuster, C., Hilfiker, R., Amft, O., Scheidhauer, A., Andrews, B., Butler, J., Kischka, U., & Ettlin, T. (2011). Best practice for motor imagery: A systematic literature review on motor imagery training elements in five different disciplines. BMC Medicine, 9, 75. https://doi.org/10.1186/1741-7015-9-75
paper.abstract: Which motor-imagery training-session elements and temporal parameters characterize interventions across education, medicine, music, psychology, and sport, particularly those reporting positive change? The review included 133 studies and 141 interventions: 79 psychology, 37 medicine, 11 sport, nine education, and five music. Designs ranged from 91 randomized trials to controlled trials, case series, and single-case designs. Athlete-specific evidence was a small portion of a highly heterogeneous cross-disciplinary corpus. Systematic search across 24 databases/registers/proceedings, extracting 17 PETTLEP-related session elements and seven temporal parameters. PEDro-based ratings were used for randomized and nonrandomized group designs and the SCED scale for case/single-case designs. Interventions were not quantitatively pooled because of heterogeneous settings and missing descriptions; analyses compared frequencies and means after categorizing 129 interventions as positive and 12 as no/negative change.
paper.tldr: This review catalogs how motor-imagery sessions have been delivered, while revealing major reporting and design limitations that constrain any simple "best-practice" prescription. Included randomized and controlled trials averaged 6 on the 10-point PEDro scale, indicating meaningful methodological limitations in much of the corpus. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Systematic search across 24 databases/registers/proceedings, extracting 17 PETTLEP-related session elements and seven temporal parameters. PEDro-based ratings were used for randomized and nonrandomized group designs and the SCED scale for case/single-case designs. Interventions were not quantitatively pooled because of heterogeneous settings and missing descriptions; analyses compared frequencies and means after categorizing 129 interventions as positive and 12 as no/negative change.
paper.findings: Included randomized and controlled trials averaged 6 on the 10-point PEDro scale, indicating meaningful methodological limitations in much of the corpus. The literature was dominated by interventions reporting positive change (129 of 141), making apparent "successful" characteristics vulnerable to publication and selection bias. Session descriptions were incomplete and heterogeneous, preventing pooled effect estimates and direct comparison of many delivery elements. Four session elements differed between positive and non-positive experiments, but success was not associated with study design, and the review did not identify a single universal group-versus-individual format. Motor-imagery ability was assessed inconsistently, preventing clear linkage between imagery ability and intervention response.
paper.limitations: Fifty-one references could not be obtained, and only 12 included interventions reported no or negative change versus 129 positive interventions. The authors selected the experimental group with the largest pre-post change when studies contained multiple groups, which can overstate favorable patterns. Most studies evaluated short-term pre-post change, with sparse follow-up. The search ended in June 2010, so the review is historically informative but not current. Descriptive averages such as session duration or weekly frequency are not causal dose-response estimates and should not be copied as prescriptions.
paper.practicalImplications: Use PETTLEP-style elements as a checklist for designing individualized imagery that resembles the target task, then test acceptability and transfer to actual performance. Assess whether the athlete can generate useful imagery, combine imagery with physical practice when appropriate, and track an objective task outcome. Avoid treating the review's average dosage or most common format as a validated protocol.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use PETTLEP-style elements as a checklist for designing individualized imagery that resembles the target task, then test acceptability and transfer to actual performance. Assess whether the athlete can generate useful imagery, combine imagery with physical practice when appropriate, and track an objective task outcome. Avoid treating the review's average dosage or most common format as a validated protocol. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
